title: Refugees, returns and reconstruction: UK, Turkey and Lebanon on a changing Syria
label: 3 November 2026 · A short picker label
summary: Experts and diplomats told the committee that Syria’s post‑Assad reality is complex: many displaced Syrians want to return but only when return is safe and dignified. Key barriers are destroyed services (schools, health, housing), lack of livelihoods, landmines and contested security in the north. Camps collapsed in 2026, raising urgent questions about third‑country nationals—including a small number of British citizens—moved into prisons in Iraq. Lebanon and Türkiye described the heavy local burden of refugees, the steps they’ve taken, and called for international support focused on rebuilding services, jobs and practical reintegration.

chapters.title: How the displacement picture has changed
chapters.takeaway: Millions remain displaced; some have gone home but most want safe, dignified returns — not a mass rush back.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How has the situation for Syrian refugees changed since the fall of Assad?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Syria lost roughly half its pre‑war population: about 6 million fled abroad and 6 million were displaced internally. After 2024 some elites returned, but most refugees are cautious: they want safety and dignity and those conditions aren't in place yet.

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Return intentions are mixed. Young people who grew up abroad may not want to go back quickly. People who have rebuilt some life in host countries often delay return until housing and work are realistic.

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: In north‑east Syria the collapse of al‑Hawl camp in early 2026 changed the picture: people were moved, some to al‑Roj, and others—particularly men—from prisons were moved into Iraq.

chapters.title: What stops people returning: services, livelihoods and safety
chapters.takeaway: Destroyed schools, hospitals, houses, landmines and lack of jobs are the main obstacles to sustainable returns.

turns.speaker: Edward Morello
turns.text: Would a big influx of returnees overload the Syrian state—are services already failing?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Yes. Cities were heavily damaged; electricity can be four hours a day. Families won't return if schools and livelihoods aren't restored. Curricular debates—about removing Ba'ath propaganda but also proposed conservative changes—are worrying parents.

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Key drivers of those who already returned were access to housing and livelihoods. Those 'on the fence' lack either, and women are especially concerned about security and freedom for their daughters.

turns.speaker: Sir John Whittingdale
turns.text: Is the new Syrian Government encouraging returns?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: They haven't blocked return; the transitional government wants reconstruction. But sanctions and banking limits still prevent Diaspora transfers that could finance rebuilding.

turns.speaker: Alex Ballinger
turns.text: How does education differ across host countries and why does it matter for return?

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Turkey integrated many children into national schools over time; Lebanon and Jordan often used 'second shifts'—shorter, lower‑resourced classes. Only about 40% of Syrian children in Lebanon attend school, creating a lost generation for rebuilding.

turns.speaker: Jessica Toale
turns.text: Is UK or donor aid being used well for these needs?

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Much aid has been short‑term humanitarian funding. That maintained lives but created parallel systems and 'NGO‑isation' rather than strengthening public schools and hospitals — leaving gaps when funding falls.

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: The UK could shift more funding to help host countries develop education and health systems that serve both refugees and locals, rather than only short emergency support.

chapters.title: Camps, chaos and the fate of third‑country nationals
chapters.takeaway: Al‑Hawl’s chaotic collapse put thousands at risk; a small number of British citizens—mainly children—remain in al‑Roj or may have been moved to Iraq.

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: Al‑Hawl collapsed in chaos; tens of thousands were affected. Prison transfers sent about 5,700 detained men and older boys to Iraqi prisons from various sites.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do we know how many British citizens were moved or remain?

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: Precise numbers are unclear. Al‑Roj holds women and children; at least 40 British citizens remain there, mostly children. It's likely a small number—perhaps a dozen at most—were moved to Iraq, but exact figures need government inquiry.

turns.speaker: Edward Morello
turns.text: Have British nationals been repatriated recently?

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: The last known repatriation I can cite was April 2025—one woman and three children. Other countries (France, Norway, Netherlands, Belgium, Australia, the US) have repatriated more actively.

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: There are also legal complications: some women may have had citizenship stripped; children generally retain nationality, and separating children from mothers raises severe protection and legal issues.

chapters.title: What Lebanon and Türkiye say they have done and need
chapters.takeaway: Lebanon and Türkiye emphasise they hosted large refugee populations, are facilitating returns, and ask for international help focused on reconstruction, services and jobs.

turns.speaker: Osman Koray Ertaş
turns.text: Türkiye hosted over 3.7 million Syrians at peak; today we protect about 2.2 million and have supported voluntary returns—770,000 since 2024. We focus on enabling safe return and on helping those who stay to integrate and work.

turns.speaker: Osman Koray Ertaş
turns.text: We see economic opportunity in a stable Syria: industrial zones, cross‑border trade, pipelines and transport links like parts of the Hejaz railway could create jobs and encourage returns.

turns.speaker: Alex Ballinger
turns.text: What about Türkiye's military presence in northern Syria?

turns.speaker: Osman Koray Ertaş
turns.text: Our forces were deployed with Syrian authority consent and focus now on training and security during transition. We want Syrian territorial integrity and will transfer civilian services to Syrian control when appropriate.

turns.speaker: Haneen Sayed
turns.text: Lebanon hosted a very large per‑capita refugee population—around 1.5 million among 4 million Lebanese—straining schools, health, water and wages. Despite this, many refugees did find dignity; we did not create formal camps but supported education shifts and health services.

turns.speaker: Haneen Sayed
turns.text: Lebanon created a return plan with IOM/UNHCR support: financial help is small—$100 per person in Lebanon and $600 on arrival in Syria—and administrative measures like removing overstay penalties. Since the plan started about a year ago, 650–700,000 have returned.

turns.speaker: Farah Berry
turns.text: Lebanon asks partners like the UK to keep funding essentials in Syria—schools, hospitals, housing—to make returns sustainable and to continue supporting vulnerable Lebanese families and institutions that have shouldered the refugee burden.

chapters.title: Policy implications and gaps for the UK
chapters.takeaway: The UK should focus aid on durable services (education, health, infrastructure), use financial expertise for reconstruction, press for consular access and plan practical repatriations for a small number of nationals.

turns.speaker: Jessica Toale
turns.text: If the UK wants to help, is emergency aid the right tool?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Not primarily. The UK should support rebuilding education and health systems and help Syria directly where safe. That will encourage returns by restoring dignity and future prospects.

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Donor funding should be longer term and aim to strengthen national systems rather than create parallel NGO services. That reduces fragility when humanitarian money drops.

turns.speaker: Alex Ballinger
turns.text: What can the UK do on the security and repatriation front—especially for British children in camps or prisons?

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: The UK should use its embassy in Iraq to find out where any British nationals are held there, provide consular support and coordinate repatriations: we have the counter‑terrorism systems to manage risk for a small number of returnees.

turns.speaker: Dan Carden
turns.text: On wider geopolitics and the role of Islam or sectarianism, what should outsiders do?

turns.speaker: Dawn Chatty
turns.text: Avoid framing Syria only through sectarian terms; many Syrians want a plural, civic state. External incentives—financial, political and technical—can encourage the new authorities to protect minorities and women's rights.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final points for the Committee?

turns.speaker: Cathrine Brun
turns.text: Prepare for a long timeline: many returns will be gradual and conditional on services, jobs and safety. Support host countries now while investing in Syria’s public systems for the future.

turns.speaker: Haneen Sayed
turns.text: Lebanon asks for continued support for services and for reconstruction in Syria so returns are sustainable; where people stay, legal pathways to work should be provided to benefit both countries.

turns.speaker: Osman Koray Ertaş
turns.text: Türkiye seeks UK partnership on financial services, education and infrastructure projects and welcomes co‑ordination to support stability and jobs in Syria.

turns.speaker: Harmonie Toros
turns.text: Urgently clarify whereabouts and welfare of third‑country nationals from the camps, press for consular access in Iraq and Syria, and prioritise children’s protection in any repatriation policy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please send further written evidence if there’s more to add.
